name: SILENCE OF THE YAMS BURGER (Served with a mild yam drizzle)

recipe.history:
True yams — Dioscorea species — are a staple crop of West Africa, where they have been cultivated for over eight thousand years and hold deep cultural, ceremonial, and economic significance across nations including Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, and Cameroon. Nigeria alone produces over seventy percent of the world's yam supply. The yam harvest is marked by annual festivals — the New Yam Festival, or Iwa Ji, among Igbo communities in Nigeria, is one of the most significant traditional celebrations on the continent, giving thanks for the crop before it is eaten. True yams have a drier, starchier, and more neutral flavor than the orange-fleshed sweet potatoes that Americans commonly call yams, and their range of varieties — from white-fleshed water yams to purple-tinged forms — represents thousands of years of agricultural selection. In West African cooking, yams are pounded into a smooth, stretchy fufu, fried as chips, roasted in embers, or incorporated into complex spiced stews.

In the American South, the word 'yam' was applied by enslaved West Africans to sweet potatoes because the orange-fleshed Ipomoea batatas was the closest available approximation to the Dioscorea yams of their home continent. This linguistic and culinary transplant created a tradition of sweet potato and 'yam' preparations in Southern cooking — candied yams, sweet potato pie, roasted yams with maple and butter — that remains central to American food culture, particularly at Thanksgiving. When these roasted and sweetened yam preparations were reduced into sauces and drizzles for the craft burger movement, they brought a distinctly American flavor history to the patty. A roasted yam and maple drizzle sauce carries the sweetness of the South, the earthiness of African agricultural tradition, and the warmth of autumn cooking in a single spoonful.

I made this burger for the first time in November, when I had a pile of garnet sweet potatoes from the farmers market and a half-bottle of good maple syrup on the counter. I roasted the yams until they were caramelized and almost collapsed, then blended them with the syrup, a little butter, and some smoked salt into a thick, sweet, slightly smoky drizzle. I put it on a burger on a whim and the combination of the savory, crusty beef and the warm, sweet drizzle was so unexpectedly harmonious that I made a note to myself to never forget this combination. The note is still on my fridge.

Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — is the only temperature at which this burger achieves its intended balance. The yam drizzle is sweet, warm, and rich. It needs a counterweight that is savory, fatty, and juicy. A medium-rare patty provides all three in abundance. The crust is bitterly caramelized, Maillard-browned, providing contrast to the sweetness of the maple. The pink interior is yielding and rich, providing substance against the lightness of the drizzle. Cook the beef past medium rare and the savory anchor disappears; what remains is sweet and dry, which is a dessert, not a burger.
ingredients: For the sweet potato brioche buns:
1/3 cup mashed roasted sweet potato, cooled
For the roasted yam and maple drizzle:
2 medium garnet sweet potatoes (or true yams if available), peeled and cubed
1/4 cup warm water or vegetable stock (to thin to drizzle consistency)
4 slices aged white cheddar or smoked gouda
instructions: 1. Make the roasted yam drizzle: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Toss sweet potato cubes with 1 tbsp melted butter and a pinch of salt; spread on a baking sheet. Roast 30–35 minutes until very soft and caramelized at the edges. Cool slightly.

2. Transfer roasted sweet potato to a blender. Add remaining 2 tbsp butter (softened), maple syrup, apple cider vinegar, smoked salt, cinnamon, and cayenne. Blend on high, adding warm water or stock gradually until a smooth, pourable but thick drizzle forms. Taste and adjust sweetness, salt, and heat. Keep warm or reheat gently.

3. Make the sweet potato brioche buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tsp sugar; bloom 10 minutes. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt. Add yeast mixture, eggs, and mashed sweet potato; mix on low 3 minutes. Add butter in cubes over medium speed, 8–10 minutes, until smooth and glossy.

4. Refrigerate dough overnight. Divide into 4 portions (about 125g each), shape into rounds, proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C), brush with egg wash, bake 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool on rack.
5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties. Press a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until deeply crusted. Flip once. Place a slice of aged cheddar or smoked gouda on each. Cook 2–3 minutes more, tenting if needed to melt cheese, until center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Rest on rack 3 minutes.
7. Split buns and toast cut-side down in skillet fat 60–90 seconds.
8. Assemble: Spread a thin spoonful of the yam drizzle on the bottom bun. Add baby spinach leaves and a tomato slice; season tomato with flaky salt. Add red onion rings.
9. Place the cheese-topped patty on top. Spoon or drizzle a generous amount of warm yam and maple drizzle over and around the patty.
10. Scatter a few fresh thyme leaves over the drizzle. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately, with extra yam drizzle on the side.
